The recent controversy surrounding Krafton and the PUBG ASIA STARS 2026 tournament centers on the severely disproportionate punishment of two Vietnamese professional players, Himass and TanVuu, and the blatant favoritism shown toward South Korean streamer Soopi. The incident began when Soopi accused the Vietnamese duo of "stream sniping"—watching live broadcasts to gain a tactical advantage—during the friendly, non-official event. Although the tournament's initial rulebook did not explicitly forbid this behavior and the Vietnamese players had reportedly asked the organizers for clarification beforehand without receiving a clear prohibition, Krafton swiftly handed Himass and TanVuu extreme penalties. They were abruptly disqualified from the tournament and permanently stripped of their PUBG Vietnam Partner status. The public outrage escalated when photographic evidence surfaced showing that Soopi herself had a browser open with the tournament broadcast during the match, strongly indicating she was committing the exact same offense. Instead of conducting a transparent and equal investigation, Krafton completely ignored the evidence against the Korean streamer, shielding her from any disciplinary action while upholding the draconian bans on the Vietnamese players. This undeniable double standard and failure to enforce rules equally provoked a massive boycott from the Vietnamese gaming community, who condemned Krafton for heavily biased management and for sacrificing the careers of two talented esports athletes to protect a home-country creator.

The ridiculous drama at the recent PUBG Asia Stars 2026 has made hitting "Uninstall" the last bit of respect I can muster for this game. If you're looking for a fair esports environment and a publisher that actually listens, look elsewhere—Krafton possesses neither.

The publisher's handling of the situation is the absolute peak of blatant favoritism. It all started in a so-called "friendly" tournament with incredibly loose rules. Two Vietnamese players, Himass and TanVuu, committed a rule violation by interacting with their stream chat during the match. They openly admitted to it and publicly apologized. In return, Krafton immediately dropped the guillotine: a permanent competitive ban and the swift revocation of their Partner status—a hasty, ruthless decision that completely ignored the context and their years of dedication to the game.

But what truly outrages me and the entire community isn't just the disproportionately harsh punishment; it's the publisher's disgusting double standards. A Korean female streamer played the victim, crying and accusing others of cheating, only for the community to expose her with crystal-clear evidence: she had a Chrome tab wide open, actively watching the tournament's live broadcast while playing. That is actual stream sniping and genuine cheating. Yet, what did Krafton do to their "golden child"? Absolutely nothing. Radio silence. No penalty, no explanation. They chose to fully condone her hypocrisy while trampling on the voices of millions of Vietnamese gamers.

It's deeply ironic for a survival game to be unable to maintain the bare minimum boundaries of fairness it set itself. The current wave of top streamers mass-deleting the game and the flood of negative reviews are a heavy but entirely deserved price for their sheer disrespect toward the player base. Krafton may have chosen to cover things up to protect one individual and save face, but they have permanently lost the respect of an entire market. PUBG right now is the textbook example of a publisher killing its own game through blind favoritism.

338,000 VND.

That is how much I spent on PUBG: BATTLEGROUNDS.

At first, I thought I was paying for a serious competitive game — one where skill, reflexes, strategy, and teamwork determine the outcome. I also believed that a major esports ecosystem like PUBG's would put fairness and transparency first.

But after everything that has happened recently, especially the controversy involving Himass and TanVuu, I have lost a lot of that trust.

KRAFTON published the results of its investigation, confirmed the use of outside information during competitive matches, and issued permanent bans from PUBG accounts and official competitions. KRAFTON also acknowledged shortcomings in its own handling and operation of the situation.

I am not defending Himass.
I am not defending TanVuu either.

If competitive rules were violated, disciplinary action is understandable. What disappoints me more is that a professional competitive system was able to let a situation like this happen in the first place.

For a competitive game, fairness is not an extra feature — it is the foundation.

I can accept losing because my opponent has better aim.
I can accept losing because my strategy was worse.
I can accept losing because I simply wasn't good enough.

What I don't want is to question whether the environment I'm playing in is actually fair.

PUBG still has its strengths. The gunplay is good, the audio is solid, and playing with friends can still be genuinely fun. But a game is more than how good the shooting feels. For a competitive title with a major esports scene, the way the developer manages the game and protects competitive integrity is also part of the product.

And that is where I feel disappointed.

I spent 338,000 VND because I believed I was buying an experience worth the money.

PUBG kept the money.

I kept a lesson:

A popular game does not automatically mean everything around it is handled perfectly.

338,000 VND may not be a lot of money to some people.

But to me, it is still money.

And if I could go back to the moment before buying it, I would probably think twice.

Not Recommended.

Not because PUBG has no value at all, but because after everything that has happened, I no longer feel that 338,000 VND was worth the trust I placed in this game.
